rv.q: But Jenny doesn’t arrive until the second half of this all-but through-sung piece, which is operatic in both emotional and musical scope. It’s fashionable currently to knock Lloyd Webber, but this is an elegant and elegiac work of interwoven musical strains, echoes and motifs, as well as that belter of a showstopper “Love Changes Everything”.
“Love Changes Everything” – declares the best-known and arguably, yes, best-loved song in Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Aspects of Love.

Now, at the tender age of 60, the nicest guy in showbiz is playing George — a rich, old walrus of love (with a dodgy ticker) in Jonathan Kent's revival of the self-same show. His character laments drooping jowls and a midriff in need of a buttress. The truth is, though, that the years have been kinder to Ball than they have been to Aspects.

For example, the leading man Alex’s creepy infatuation with a young girl, who’s now older, at 18. (It’s still queasy, though.) The show explores, over a 20-year post-war period, love’s vario us aspects - especially the horizontal. Jamie Bogyo is the dull but handsome Alex, the young lover of actress Rose (Laura Pitt-Pulford, a total pro).

Part of me thinks I should be trying to whip up a pitchfork-wielding mob to drive it out of town. Another part of me thinks… eh, it’s quite good fun if you can avoid thinking too hard about what’s actually going on.
It’s hard to see why Andrew Lloyd Webber thought this creepy and downright silly chamber musical was a good idea in 1989, let alone ripe for revival now.

It is, without doubt, a well-oiled show, easy on the eye and ear. John Macfarlane’s gliding screens reveal gorgeous sets and the voices are strong across the board. But for all its smoothness, there is a preposterousness to it.

Whether the piece, with all its polite operatic borrowings, is really worth bringing back to the West End is another matter. Lloyd Webber deserves some good fortune after all the insults hurled at his version of Cinderella, which is closing on Broadway (now as Bad Cinderella) after an unfair battering from the New York critics.

Jonathan Kent’s production features a lead performance by original cast member Michael Ball, who made something of a signature tune of the earworm number Love Changes Everything. Ball certainly has his superfans. But it would take more than his golden-syrup vocals and twinkly charm to make wading through this sugary sludge worthwhile.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Lyric Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.

sg.vl: Good sound, check the seat map
sg.ra: Lyric Theatre's own seating notes flag possible obstructed views from the rear orchestra — sound still carries well, but check the seat map before booking here.
At 1,930 seats, Lyric Theatre is one of the larger Broadway houses — far side mezzanine seats sit well off-axis and a long way from the stage.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's largest houses (1,930 seats across four levels), the Lyric's sheer scale means rear orchestra and mezzanine seats sit far from the stage, with sightline obstructions from balcony overhangs. Acoustics are solid and the theater's modern construction makes it well-suited for spectacle productions.

acc.note: 42nd St entrance at street level with elevator to Orchestra and Dress Circle. No elevator to Balcony.
